
The duplicate check is *0*, the **special police DF** has **450** records, and the **special joined DF** has **450**, with no warning this time. The NA proportion is *0.7688889*, or about 76.9%, which is higher than before. Both NA proportions come to 346 records without a population, so the same records are still unmatched, and they now make up a bigger share of fewer rows. A record now goes without a population only when its city and state have no special jurisdiction row that has one.

### Check why the state police records didn't match

Now, back to the state police records, since none of them got a population. The `sum()` with the `!is.na()` counts the **state joined DF** rows that matched an *agency_name*. Then, `distinct` with `nrow` counts the unique values in *city_match* and in *agency_city_match*, and the `unique()` with `%in%` and `sum` counts how many homicide values show up anywhere in *agency_city_match*, no matter the state.

```{r special-join-diagnostics}
#| warning: true

# Check the primary state LE join and state subsets for real matches.

#== count agency match rows ==
sum(
  !is.na(
    state_le_joined$agency_name
  )
)

#== count homicide_state_le cities ==
homicide_state_le %>%
  distinct(
    city_match
  ) %>%
  nrow()

#== count geojson_state_le cities ==
geojson_state_le %>%
  distinct(
    agency_city_match
  ) %>%
  nrow()

#== count alike + existing cities ==
sum(
  unique(
    homicide_state_le$city_match
  ) %in%
    geojson_state_le$agency_city_match
)
```

Here the results show that *0* rows matched an agency name. The **state police DF** has *780* distinct city values, and the **state agency DF** has *1,456*, but *0* of the homicide values show up on the agency side at all. So, the state isn't the problem, since the homicide side's values never look like the agency side's city names.

To see why, the `distinct()` with `slice_sample(n = 15)` pulls 15 random values from *city* in the **state police DF** and from *agency_city* in the **state agency DF**. Since there's no `set.seed()`, the sample changes each time the script runs.

```{r special-join-diagnostics-2}
#| warning: true

# Compare the real city values to cities that overlap.

#== homicide-side sample ==
homicide_state_le %>%
  distinct(
    city
  ) %>%
  # (Batra, et al., 2021)
  slice_sample(n = 15)

#== geojson-side sample ==
geojson_state_le %>%
  distinct(
    agency_city
  ) %>%
  # (Batra, et al., 2021)
  slice_sample(n = 15)
```

Interestingly, *city* holds the names of state police units, like county units, troops, and highway patrol, rather than city names, mostly written as *"State Police:"* followed by a county, while *agency_city* holds ordinary city names in capital letters. So, the state police records have no city to match on and will stay unmatched.

<br>

## Match county police records by department name

Next up are the county police records. The `filter()` keeps the *"County police"* records from the **subset DF**, with the same `rename()` and `mutate()` as the state and special police, saving them as the **county police DF** (`homicide_county_police`), and `nrow()` counts them.

```{r county-police-subset}
#| warning: true

# Filter the homicide dataset for the county police-type agencies.

#== homicide subset ==
homicide_county_police <- homicide_subset %>%
  filter(
    Agentype == "County police"
  ) %>%
  rename(
    city = Agency
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # (Sanderson, 2024)
    city_match = toupper(
      trimws(city)
    )
  )

#== check row count ==
nrow(homicide_county_police)
```

The **county police DF** has *6,237* records.

But first, I'll check whether *city* actually holds city names here. The `distinct()` with `slice_sample(n = 15)` pulls 15 random values from *city* in the **county police DF** and from *agency_city* in the **deduplicated DF** from the municipal join. Since there's no `set.seed()`, the sample changes each time the script runs.

```{r county-police-sample}
#| warning: true

# Check the city values are also in Agency.

#== homicide-side sample ==
homicide_county_police %>%
  distinct(
    city
  ) %>%
  # (Batra, et al., 2021)
  slice_sample(n = 15)

#== geojson-side sample ==
geojson_municipal_dedup %>%
  distinct(
    agency_city
  ) %>%
  # (Batra, et al., 2021)
  slice_sample(n = 15)
```

*city* holds department names in title case, mostly a county name followed by *"County Police Department,"* not city names, while *agency_city* holds ordinary city names in capital letters. A few are shortened or written as just a county or borough. So, a city match won't work, but the department names might match the agency side's *agency_name* instead.

Then, `mutate` with `toupper` and `trimws` adds *name_match* to the **county police DF**, and the same `mutate` adds *agency_name_match* from *agency_name* to the **derived DF**, saving it as the **agency name DF** (`geojson_name_check`), with every agency type kept. The `unique()` with `%in%` and `sum` counts how many department names show up exactly in *agency_name_match*, and the `distinct()` with `nrow()` counts the total number of department names.

```{r county-police-name-check}
#| warning: true

# Check county police department names match geojson agency_name instead of city.

#== normalize department name ==
homicide_county_police <- homicide_county_police %>%
  mutate(
    # (Sanderson, 2024)
    name_match = toupper(
      trimws(city)
    )
  )

#== normalize agency_name across ==
geojson_name_check <- geojson_derived %>%
  mutate(
    # (Sanderson, 2024)
    agency_name_match = toupper(
      trimws(agency_name)
    )
  )

#== count alike + existing department names ==
sum(
  unique(
    homicide_county_police$name_match
  ) %in%
    geojson_name_check$agency_name_match
)

#== total distinct department names ==
homicide_county_police %>%
  distinct(
    name_match
  ) %>%
  nrow()
```

Only *17* of the *47* department names match exactly, so 30 are still unmatched.

To see why, the `filter()` with `!` and `%in%` lists the department names with no exact match, and `print(n = 30)` shows up to 30 names. Then, `filter` with the `grepl()` lists the distinct names in the **agency name DF** that are filed as *"LOCAL POLICE DEPARTMENT"* and include *"COUNTY,"* and `print(n = 30)` shows the first 30.

```{r county-police-name-diagnostics}
#| warning: true

# Compare department names to geojson county-related agency names.

#== names w/no exact match ==
homicide_county_police %>%
  distinct(
    name_match
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !name_match %in% geojson_name_check$agency_name_match
  ) %>%
  print(n = 30)

#== county names filed as local police ==
geojson_name_check %>%
  filter(
    agency_type == "LOCAL POLICE DEPARTMENT",
    # (Robinson, et al., 2026)
    grepl(
      "COUNTY",
      agency_name_match
    )
  ) %>%
  distinct(
    agency_name_match
  ) %>%
  print(n = 30)
```

All *30* unmatched names print, and the agency side has *358* local police names that include "COUNTY." Many of them are the same departments with extra words at the end, such as *"HEADQUARTERS,"* with or without a dash before it, and the list also has jails and sheriff's offices filed as local police.

Then, I'll strip those extra words. The `mutate()` adds *agency_name_base* to the **agency name DF**, where the first `sub()` with a regular expression (regex) pattern `" - .*$"` removes everything from the first dash with spaces around it to the end of the name, and the second `sub()` with `" HEADQUARTERS$"` removes *"HEADQUARTERS"* only when it's at the end, since `$` marks the end of the name. The same `unique()` with `%in%` and `sum()` counts the matches again, now against *agency_name_base*.

```{r county-police-name-normalize}
#| warning: true

# Strip trailing qualifiers after the first " - " from geojson agency names.

#== strip first match w/regex ==
geojson_name_check <- geojson_name_check %>%
  mutate(
    agency_name_base = agency_name_match %>%
      # (Hemken, 2024)
      sub(
        " - .*$",
        "",
        .
      ) %>%
      # (Hemken, 2024)
      sub(
        " HEADQUARTERS$",
        "",
        .
      )
  )

#== re-count alike, stripped names ==
sum(
  unique(
    homicide_county_police$name_match
  ) %in%
    geojson_name_check$agency_name_base
)
```

*30* department names match now, 13 more than before, which leaves 17 unmatched.

The same `filter()` with `!` and `%in%`, now against *agency_name_base*, lists the names that are still unmatched, and `print(n = 20)` shows up to 20.

```{r county-police-name-normalize-diagnostics}
#| warning: true

# List department names still unmatched after stripping geojson suffixes.

#== names w/no match after stripping ==
homicide_county_police %>%
  distinct(
    name_match
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !name_match %in% geojson_name_check$agency_name_base
  ) %>%
  print(n = 20)
```

The *17* names left are a mix: some are shortened or written another way, like *"MIAMI-DADE"* and *"HENRICO COUNTY POLICE D,"* and others are full department names that just don't show up on the agency side with the same wording.

### Find the remaining names by their roots

Next, I'll search for the 17 names by a shorter root, such as *"MIAMI-DADE"* or *"HENRICO,"* in case the agency side words them differently, and save the 17 roots as `unmatched_roots`. The `paste()` with `collapse = "|"` joins them into one search pattern, where `|` means "or," and the `filter()` with `grepl` keeps every *agency_name_base* that contains any of them. The `distinct()` with `print(n = 40)` shows the first 40.

```{r county-police-name-remaining-check}
#| warning: true

# Search roots for name variants pulled from the 17 unmatched departments.

#== create an unmatched name list ==
unmatched_roots <- c(
  "NORTH SLOPE",
  "BRISTOL BAY",
  "MIAMI-DADE",
  "CHATHAM",
  "GREENE",
  "WARREN",
  "BOONE",
  "JEFFERSON",
  "WOODFORD",
  "MONTGOMERY",
  "PRINCE GEORGE",
  "GENESEE",
  "ST. LOUIS",
  "ESSEX",
  "WESTCHESTER",
  "GARFIELD",
  "HENRICO"
)

#== find names containing the root names ==
geojson_name_check %>%
  filter(
    # (Robinson, et al., 2026; Bobbit, 2023)
    grepl(
      paste(
        unmatched_roots,
        collapse = "|"
      ),
      agency_name_base
    )
  ) %>%
  distinct(
    agency_name_base
  ) %>%
  print(n = 40)
```

The search found *158* distinct names, too many to check by eye, since short roots like *"WARREN"* and *"JEFFERSON"* also pick up sheriff's offices, jails, and city police departments with similar names.

So, the same search adds *"LOCAL POLICE DEPARTMENT"* to the `filter()`, since that's where the county police names were filed, and `print(n = 40)` shows the first 40.

```{r county-police-name-remaining-narrow}
#| warning: true

# Search root names against "LOCAL POLICE DEPARTMENT" only.

#== search distinct root names ==
geojson_name_check %>%
  filter(
    agency_type == "LOCAL POLICE DEPARTMENT",
    # (Robinson, et al., 2026; Bobbitt, 2023)
    grepl(
      paste(
        unmatched_roots,
        collapse = "|"
      ),
      agency_name_base
    )
  ) %>%
  distinct(
    agency_name_base
  ) %>%
  print(n = 40)
```

That cut the list to *82* names, but it still has town, township, and city departments from other places, such as *"WARREN TOWNSHIP POLICE DEPARTMENT"* and *"CHATHAM BOROUGH POLICE DEPARTMENT,"* so I'll narrow it down by state.

The `filter()` with `!` and `%in%` keeps the **county police DF** records that are still unmatched, and the `distinct()` pairs each name with its state, saving the **unmatched DF** (`unmatched_bystate`).

```{r county-police-name-remaining-bystate}
#| warning: true

# Pair unmatched names with state.

#== unmatched names+state ==
unmatched_bystate <- homicide_county_police %>%
  filter(
    !name_match %in% geojson_name_check$agency_name_base
  ) %>%
  distinct(
    name_match,
    state
  )

#== view the pairing ==
unmatched_bystate
```

The **unmatched DF** has *17* rows, one for each name, so each unmatched name comes from only one state.

Then, the same local police search adds `agency_state %in% unmatched_bystate$state` to the `filter()`, so it only keeps names from those states. The `distinct()` lists each state and name pair, `arrange` sorts them by state, and `print(n = 59)` shows all of them.

```{r county-police-name-remaining-bystate-check}
#| warning: true

# Check roots against geojson against its relevant states.

#== names by state ==
geojson_name_check %>%
  filter(
    agency_type == "LOCAL POLICE DEPARTMENT",
    agency_state %in% unmatched_bystate$state,
    # (Robinson, et al., 2026; Bobbitt, 2023)
    grepl(
      paste(
        unmatched_roots,
        collapse = "|"
      ),
      agency_name_base
    )
  ) %>%
  distinct(
    agency_state,
    agency_name_base
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    agency_state
  ) %>%
  print(n = 59)
```

The list has *59* state and name pairs. Comparing each pair to its homicide name and state, some of the 17 names have a likely match, such as *"MIAMI-DADE COUNTY POLICE DEPARTMENT"* in Florida and *"HENRICO COUNTY DIVISION OF POLICE"* in Virginia. The others have no county police match in their state, only city or township departments, jails, or other offices with a similar name, or nothing at all, like *"GARFIELD COUNTY"* in Utah.

Since some likely matches show up under more than one version of their name, the `filter()` keeps those names in Alaska, Florida, Georgia, and Maryland, and the `distinct()` with `arrange` lists each name with its *agency_population*, sorted by state and name with the largest population first, and `print(n = 40)` shows all of them.

```{r county-police-remaining-candidates}
#| warning: true

# View population per candidate.

#== candidate populations ==
geojson_name_check %>%
  filter(
    agency_state %in%
      c(
        "AK",
        "FL",
        "GA",
        "MD"
      ),
    # (Robinson, et al., 2026)
    grepl(
      "NORTH SLOPE|MIAMI-DADE|CHATHAM|MONTGOMERY COUNTY|PRINCE GEORGE",
      agency_name_base
    )
  ) %>%
  distinct(
    agency_state,
    agency_name_base,
    agency_population
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    agency_state,
    agency_name_base,
    desc(
      agency_population
    )
  ) %>%
  print(n = 40)
```

The *28* rows show that each likely match has one version with a population and others without, such as *"MIAMI-DADE COUNTY POLICE DEPARTMENT"* with *4,424* and an NA, while the district offices under *"MONTGOMERY COUNTY DEPARTMENT OF POLICE"* are all NA. For North Slope, only the name ending in *"NORTH SLOPE BOROUGH CORRECTIONAL CENTER"* has a population (*59*), and the hyphenated *"SAVANNAH-CHATHAM METROPOLITAN POLICE DEPARTMENT"* has *757* while the version without the hyphen is NA, so the lookup will point to the version that has a population.

Then, the same steps list the last three likely matches in Alaska, New York, and Virginia, with `print(n = 20)`.

```{r county-police-remaining-candidates-2}
#| warning: true

# View population for the remaining unverified candidates.

#== candidate populations ==
geojson_name_check %>%
  filter(
    agency_state %in%
      c(
        "AK",
        "NY",
        "VA"
      ),
    # (Robinson, et al., 2026)
    grepl(
      "BRISTOL BAY|WESTCHESTER|HENRICO",
      agency_name_base
    )
  ) %>%
  distinct(
    agency_state,
    agency_name_base,
    agency_population
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    agency_state,
    agency_name_base,
    desc(
      agency_population
    )
  ) %>%
  print(n = 20)
```

The *6* rows give Bristol Bay a population of *9* and Westchester's *"DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC SAFETY"* *345*, but every Henrico row is NA, so Henrico's records will still have no population, even after its name is corrected.

### Correct the names and join

Now, the `tribble()` builds a lookup table (`county_police_lookup`) pairing the homicide names in *name_match* with the agency side's spelling in *name_corrected*, such as *"MIAMI-DADE"* to *"MIAMI-DADE COUNTY POLICE DEPARTMENT"* and *"PRINCE GEORGE'S COUNTY POLICE DEPARTMENT"* to *"PRINCE GEORGES COUNTY POLICE."*

```{r county-police-lookup}
#| warning: true

# Build lookup table to map to the homicide department names.

#== create homicide department name lookup ==
# (Mahr, 2017)
county_police_lookup <- tibble::tribble(
  ~name_match                                , ~name_corrected                                                                   ,
  "NORTH SLOPE BOROUGH"                      , "NORTH SLOPE BOROUGH POLICE DEPARTMENT / NORTH SLOPE BOROUGH CORRECTIONAL CENTER" ,
  "BRISTOL BAY BOROUGH"                      , "BRISTOL BAY BOROUGH POLICE DEPARTMENT / KING SALMON JAIL"                        ,
  "MIAMI-DADE"                               , "MIAMI-DADE COUNTY POLICE DEPARTMENT"                                             ,
  "CHATHAM COUNTY POLICE DEPARTMENT"         , "SAVANNAH-CHATHAM METROPOLITAN POLICE DEPARTMENT"                                 ,
  "MONTGOMERY COUNTY POLICE DEPARTMENT"      , "MONTGOMERY COUNTY DEPARTMENT OF POLICE"                                          ,
  "PRINCE GEORGE'S COUNTY POLICE DEPARTMENT" , "PRINCE GEORGES COUNTY POLICE"                                                    ,
  "WESTCHESTER PUBLIC SAFETY"                , "WESTCHESTER COUNTY DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC SAFETY"                                  ,
  "HENRICO COUNTY POLICE D"                  , "HENRICO COUNTY DIVISION OF POLICE"
)
```

Then, `left_join` adds *name_corrected* to the **county police DF**, `mutate` with `coalesce` uses the corrected name where there is one and keeps the original everywhere else, and the `select()` with a minus sign drops *name_corrected*. On the agency side, the `filter()` drops the rows without a population, and `group_by` with `slice_max` keeps the row with the largest *agency_population* for each *agency_name_base*, with `with_ties = FALSE`, then the `ungroup()`, saving the **county police deduplicated DF** (`geo_county_police_dedup`).

```{r county-police-apply-lookup}
#| warning: true

# Apply lookup, then join deduplicated population by exact name match.

#== apply lookup to homicide side ==
homicide_county_police <- homicide_county_police %>%
  left_join(
    county_police_lookup,
    by = "name_match"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # (Harris, 2024)
    name_match = coalesce(
      name_corrected,
      name_match
    )
  ) %>%
  select(
    -name_corrected
  )

#== dedupe geojson by exact name, keep largest population ==
geo_county_police_dedup <- geojson_name_check %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(
      agency_population
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(
    agency_name_base
  ) %>%
  # (Batra, et al., 2021)
  slice_max(
    agency_population,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```

Lastly, the `left_join()` adds *agency_population* from the **county police deduplicated DF** by matching *name_match* to *agency_name_base*, saving over the **county police DF**. The `nrow()` checks that the row count held, and `mean` with `is.na` gives the NA proportion, which works the same as dividing the `sum()` by `nrow`.

```{r county-police-join}
#| warning: true

# Join deduplicated population onto homicide by name.

#== join subsets ==
homicide_county_police <- homicide_county_police %>%
  left_join(
    geo_county_police_dedup %>%
      select(
        agency_name_base,
        agency_population
      ),
    by = c(
      "name_match" = "agency_name_base"
    )
  )

#== check row count held ==
nrow(
  homicide_county_police
)

#== check NA rate ==
mean(
  is.na(
    homicide_county_police$agency_population
  )
)
```

The **county police DF** still has *6,237* records, so the join didn't add any rows, and the NA proportion is *0.1544012*, or about 15.4%, which comes to 963 records. These are records whose department has no row with a population on the agency side, like the names with no county police match and Henrico.

<br>

## Agency types with no match

The last three agency types, *"Tribal,"* *"Regional police,"* and *"Primary federal LE,"* don't get a join at all. The `filter()` with `%in%` keeps their records from the **subset DF**, with the same `rename()` and `mutate()` as before, and the `mutate()` also adds *agency_population* as `NA_real_`, a numeric NA, so these records have the same columns as the other groups when they're all combined. That's saved as the **no-match DF** (`homicide_no_match`), and `nrow()` counts the records.

```{r no-match-agentypes}
#| warning: true

# Create a subset of the no-match Agentypes, and retain their NA values.

#== homicide subset ==
homicide_no_match <- homicide_subset %>%
  filter(
    Agentype %in%
      c(
        "Tribal",
        "Regional police",
        "Primary federal LE"
      )
  ) %>%
  rename(
    city = Agency
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # (Sanderson, 2024)
    city_match = toupper(
      trimws(city)
    ),
    agency_population = NA_real_
  )

#== check row count ==
nrow(homicide_no_match)
```

The **no-match DF** has *423* records, and every one of them has an NA *agency_population*.

<br>

## Combine the agency groups

Before combining, each group needs its location in one column with the same name. The `rename()` changes *city* to *location_match* in the **joined DF**, the **state joined DF**, the **special joined DF**, the **county police DF**, and the **no-match DF**, and it changes *county_agency* to *location_match* in the **sheriff joined DF**, since the sheriff records were matched by county instead of city.

```{r pipeline-location-rename}
#| warning: true

# Rename location column to one shared name.

#== standardize name on the 5 city-based pieces ==
municipal_joined <- municipal_joined %>%
  rename(
    location_match = city
  )

sheriff_joined <- sheriff_joined %>%
  rename(
    location_match = county_agency
  )

state_le_joined <- state_le_joined %>%
  rename(
    location_match = city
  )

special_joined <- special_joined %>%
  rename(
    location_match = city
  )

homicide_county_police <- homicide_county_police %>%
  rename(
    location_match = city
  )

homicide_no_match <- homicide_no_match %>%
  rename(
    location_match = city
  )
```

Then, the `Reduce()` with `intersect` compares the `names()` of all six groups two at a time, so only the column names found in every group are left, saving them as `common_cols`. The `bind_rows()` stacks the six groups into one, with `select` and `all_of(common_cols)` keeping only the shared columns from each, saving the **final DF** (`homicide_final`), and `nrow()` counts the records.

```{r pipeline-reassembly}
#| warning: true

# Keep the common columns of the six subsets, then combine them.

#== find columns ==
# (Prabhakaran, 2026d)
common_cols <- Reduce(
  intersect,
  list(
    names(municipal_joined),
    names(sheriff_joined),
    names(state_le_joined),
    names(special_joined),
    names(homicide_county_police),
    names(homicide_no_match)
  )
)

#== combine using only the shared columns ==
homicide_final <- bind_rows(
  select(
    municipal_joined,
    # (Olumide, 2025)
    all_of(common_cols)
  ),
  select(
    sheriff_joined,
    # (Olumide, 2025)
    all_of(common_cols)
  ),
  select(
    state_le_joined,
    # (Olumide, 2025)
    all_of(common_cols)
  ),
  select(
    special_joined,
    # (Olumide, 2025)
    all_of(common_cols)
  ),
  select(
    homicide_county_police,
    # (Olumide, 2025)
    all_of(common_cols)
  ),
  select(
    homicide_no_match,
    # (Olumide, 2025)
    all_of(common_cols)
  )
)

#== check row count ==
nrow(homicide_final)
```

The **final DF** has **197,147** records, the same as the **subset DF**, so every record landed in exactly one group, with none lost or repeated.

To double-check, printing `common_cols` lists the shared column names, and adding up the `nrow()` of all six groups gives the expected total.

```{r pipeline-reassembly-check}
#| warning: true

# Confirm agency_population survived, and totals reconcile.

#== show common columns ==
common_cols

#== check total row counts ==
nrow(municipal_joined) +
  nrow(sheriff_joined) +
  nrow(state_le_joined) +
  nrow(special_joined) +
  nrow(homicide_county_police) +
  nrow(homicide_no_match)
```

There are 30 shared columns, including *location_match* and *agency_population*, so the population survived the combine, and the six groups add up to *197,147*, matching the **final DF**. Columns that only some groups have, like the matching columns and the agency-side columns, were left out.

Lastly, the `mean()` with `is.na` gives the NA proportion of *location_match*.

```{r pipeline-location-check}
#| warning: true

# Check the NA rates in the homicide_final subset.

#== location_match col ==
mean(
  is.na(
    homicide_final$location_match
  )
)
```

The NA proportion is *0*, so every record has a location after the rename.

<br>

## Filter to 2017 through 2020 and add the weather

The **final DF** still holds records from every year in the raw data, but the **weather DF** only covers 2017 to 2020. The `filter()` with `%in%` keeps only the records whose *record_year* falls in `2017:2020`, and `nrow` counts what's left. You should know I added this filter after running `diagnostic-NA-data`, the last chunk in this stage, since the weather join came back mostly NA while every year was still in the data.

```{r homicide-year-filter}
#| warning: true

# Filter the final homicide data to the four years (2017-2020).

#== filter year range ==
homicide_final <- homicide_final %>%
  filter(
    record_year %in% 2017:2020
  )

#== check row count ==
nrow(homicide_final)
```

Now the **final DF** went from *197,147* records to *15,766*, so the filter removed 181,381 records from the other years.

So, the **weather DF** has one row per state for each day, with the date in *daily_time*, while the **final DF** has *record_month* and *record_year* instead. Inside the `mutate()`, `lubridate::month()` with `label = TRUE` and `abbr = FALSE` gives the full month name, and the `as.character()` turns it into plain text, since the `month()` returns a factor that wouldn't match the text in the **final DF**. Then, `lubridate::year()` pulls out the year, and both are saved under the same column names the **final DF** uses. To check them, `distinct()` and `arrange()` list each month and year pair once, and `print(n = 20)` shows the first 20.

```{r weather-extract-monthyear}
#| warning: true

# Get the full month name and numerical year from the daily_time variable.

#== extract + format month/year ==
weather_renamed <- weather_renamed %>%
  mutate(
    record_month = as.character(
      lubridate::month(
        daily_time,
        label = TRUE,
        abbr = FALSE
      )
    ),
    record_year = lubridate::year(
      daily_time
    )
  )

#== display the results ==
weather_renamed %>%
  distinct(
    record_month,
    record_year
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    record_year,
    record_month
  ) %>%
  print(n = 20)
```

Based on the run, the tibble header shows *48* month and year pairs, which is 12 months for each of the four years. The months are listed alphabetically, starting with *"April"* and *"August,"* since they're plain text, not a factor.

Next, the `group_by()` groups the **weather DF** by *state*, *record_month*, and *record_year*, and the `summarise()` turns each group's daily rows into one row. It uses the `mean()` for *temp_2m_avg* and *relative_humidity_2m_avg* and `sum` for *rain_sum* and *snowfall_sum*, since temperature and humidity make sense as a monthly average, while rain and snowfall add up over the month. The `.groups = "drop"` removes the grouping afterward, saving the **monthly weather DF** (`weather_monthly`), and the `nrow()` counts the rows.

```{r weather-monthly-agg}
#| warning: true

# Aggregate daily weather into one row per state, month, and year.

#== group + summarise ==
weather_monthly <- weather_renamed %>%
  group_by(
    state,
    record_month,
    record_year
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    temp_2m_avg = mean(temp_2m_avg),
    relative_humidity_2m_avg = mean(relative_humidity_2m_avg),
    rain_sum = sum(rain_sum),
    snowfall_sum = sum(snowfall_sum),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

#== check row count ==
nrow(weather_monthly)
```

The **monthly weather DF** has *2,832* rows. Divided by the *48* month-year pairs, that's 59 rows for each month and year, one for each state.

Then, `left_join` adds the **monthly weather DF** to the **final DF** by *state*, *record_month*, and *record_year*, so each record gets the weather for its state in the month and year the homicide happened. After that, `nrow` counts the records, and the `mean()` with `is.na` gives the NA proportion of *temp_2m_avg*.

```{r join-weather-to-final}
#| warning: true

# Join the final homicide data with the monthly weather data by state, month, and year.

#== left join ==
homicide_final <- homicide_final %>%
  left_join(
    weather_monthly,
    by = c(
      "state",
      "record_month",
      "record_year"
    )
  )

#== display row count ==
nrow(homicide_final)

#== display NA rate ==
mean(
  is.na(
    homicide_final$temp_2m_avg
  )
)
```

Happily, the results show that the **final DF** still has *15,766* records, so the join didn't add any rows. And the NA proportion is *0*, which means every record found its weather.

Just to preface, I wrote this last chunk when the weather join first came back with about 92% of its weather values as NA, to see whether the state and month values in the two DFs didn't line up. First, `distinct` and `arrange` list each *state* in the **weather DF**, and `print(n = 60)` shows all of them. The same two functions run on the **final DF**, but with no column named inside them, so they keep each unique record and print whole rows instead of a list of states. Lastly, the two `setdiff()` calls look for month names that show up in one DF but not the other, checking both directions.

```{r diagnostic-NA-data}
#| warning: true

# Look for state or month mismatches between the weather and homicide data.

#== check weather state values ==
weather_renamed %>%
  distinct(
    state
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    state
  ) %>%
  print(n = 60)

#== check distinct homicide rows ==
homicide_final %>%
  distinct() %>%
  arrange() %>%
  print(n = 60)

#== check month name values ==
setdiff(
  homicide_final$record_month,
  weather_monthly$record_month
)

setdiff(
  weather_monthly$record_month,
  homicide_final$record_month
)
```

After the run, the **weather DF** has *59* state values, written as two-letter abbreviations, including DC and territories like *"PR"* and *"GU"*. The second check prints *15,725* rows across *34* columns instead of state values, 41 fewer than the *15,766* records, since the `distinct()` drops records that are exact copies of another record in every column. Most importantly, both `setdiff()` calls return `character(0)`, so every month name in one DF shows up in the other.

<br>

## Correct county names to Census spellings

Because I'll be using the U.S. Census Bureau's state and county shapes from the `tigris` package during the analysis, each county name in *CNTYFIPS* needs to match its Census name exactly, so every record can be paired with its county shape. Eleven county names in *CNTYFIPS* are spelled differently from the Census Bureau's 2020 county names, such as *De Kalb, GA* instead of *DeKalb, GA*, and municipal police records in Richmond and Roanoke, Virginia, are listed under the county names even though they belong to the independent cities of the same names. A lookup table pairs each misspelled name with its Census spelling; a second step moves the Richmond and Roanoke city records to their city names, and both corrections are applied before the final data is saved.

```{r cntyfips-census-names-lookup}
#| warning: true

# Recode differently spelled county names from the 2020 Census names.

#== create county Census name lookup ==
# (Mahr, 2017)
cntyfips_lookup <- tibble::tribble(
  ~CNTYFIPS              , ~cntyfips_corrected        ,
  "De Kalb, GA"          , "DeKalb, GA"               ,
  "De Kalb, MO"          , "DeKalb, MO"               ,
  "De Soto, FL"          , "DeSoto, FL"               ,
  "De Witt, TX"          , "DeWitt, TX"               ,
  "La Porte, IN"         , "LaPorte, IN"              ,
  "La Salle, IL"         , "LaSalle, IL"              ,
  "La Salle, LA"         , "LaSalle, LA"              ,
  "Dona Ana, NM"         , "Doña Ana, NM"             ,
  "Carson City city, NV" , "Carson City, NV"          ,
  "District of Columbia" , "District of Columbia, DC" ,
  "Clifton Forge, VA"    , "Alleghany, VA"
)

#== apply corrections ==
homicide_final <- homicide_final %>%
  left_join(
    cntyfips_lookup,
    by = "CNTYFIPS"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # (Harris, 2024)
    CNTYFIPS = coalesce(
      cntyfips_corrected,
      CNTYFIPS
    )
  ) %>%
  select(-cntyfips_corrected)
```

```{r cntyfips-census-names-reassign}
#| warning: true

# Move Virginia city records to their city names.

#== move Virginia city police records to their city names ==
homicide_final <- homicide_final %>%
  mutate(
    # (Matt, 2020; Hadley, 2024)
    CNTYFIPS = case_when(
      CNTYFIPS == "Richmond, VA" &
        Agentype == "Municipal police" ~ "Richmond city, VA",
      CNTYFIPS == "Roanoke, VA" &
        Agentype == "Municipal police" ~ "Roanoke city, VA",
      TRUE ~ CNTYFIPS
    )
  )

#== check rows held ==
nrow(
  homicide_final
)

#== check corrected names and their records ==
homicide_final %>%
  filter(
    CNTYFIPS %in%
      c(
        cntyfips_lookup$cntyfips_corrected,
        "Richmond city, VA",
        "Roanoke city, VA"
      )
  ) %>%
  count(CNTYFIPS)
```

After the corrections, the data still has *15,766* records, so no rows were added or lost. All *13* corrected names now appear, including *43* Richmond city and *9* Roanoke city records that were moved from their county names.

<br>

## Save, reload, and recheck the final data

With the year filter and weather in place, `arrow::write_parquet()` saves the **final DF** as a Parquet file, and `here::here()` builds its path to the processed data folder. Parquet keeps each column's data type, so the file reads back the same way it was saved.

```{r final-homicide-to-parquet}
#| warning: true

# Save the finalized, year-filtered, weather-joined homicide dataset as a Parquet file.

#== write to processed data folder ==
# (Olumide, 2025)
arrow::write_parquet(
  homicide_final,
  here::here(
    "data",
    "processed",
    "homicide_final.parquet"
  )
)
```

Then, `arrow::read_parquet()` reads the file back in, saving it as the **reloaded DF** (`homicide_final_reloaded`), and the `==` compares the `nrow()` of both DFs to make sure no records were lost or added when saving and reading the file.

```{r load-homicide-parquet}
#| warning: true

# Reload the saved Parquet dataset.

#== read data ==
# (Gillespie, 2021)
homicide_final_reloaded <- arrow::read_parquet(
  # (Olumide, 2025)
  here::here(
    "data",
    "processed",
    "homicide_final.parquet"
  )
)

#== compare row count ==
(nrow(
  homicide_final_reloaded
) ==
  nrow(homicide_final))
```

It prints *TRUE*, so the **reloaded DF** has the same number of records as the **final DF**.

Next, I'll recheck eight columns in the **reloaded DF**: the two race columns, four weather columns, *agency_population*, and *location_match*. The `select()` keeps only those columns, while `glimpse()` shows each column's data type and first few values. The second `select()` keeps the same columns, and `summarise` with `across(everything(), ...)` applies `sum` to `is.na` for each column, counting its NA values; `.` represents each column in turn.

```{r reverify-homicide-parquet}
#| warning: true

# Check the data types and null counts.

#== select the columns ==
homicide_final_reloaded %>%
  select(
    victim_racial_construct,
    offender_racial_construct,
    temp_2m_avg,
    relative_humidity_2m_avg,
    rain_sum,
    snowfall_sum,
    agency_population,
    location_match
  ) %>%
  glimpse()

#== display nulls/columns ==
homicide_final_reloaded %>%
  select(
    victim_racial_construct,
    offender_racial_construct,
    temp_2m_avg,
    relative_humidity_2m_avg,
    rain_sum,
    snowfall_sum,
    agency_population,
    location_match
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    # (Barter, 2020)
    across(
      everything(),
      ~ sum(
        is.na(.)
      )
    )
  )
```

The `glimpse()` shows *15,766* records across *8* columns. The race columns and *location_match* are ``, and the weather columns and *agency_population* are ``. In the NA counts, the first six columns all show *0*, but *agency_population* and *location_match* are cut off under *"2 more variables,"* so their counts don't print here.

After that, `count` gives the number of records in each group of *victim_racial_construct* and then *offender_racial_construct*, to see how balanced the groups are. Lastly, `summarise` with `n_distinct()` counts how many different values *location_match* has.

```{r category-balance-and-power}
#| warning: true

# Check the victim and offender race category counts.

#== victim outcome balance ==
homicide_final_reloaded %>%
  count(victim_racial_construct)

#== offender race balance ==
homicide_final_reloaded %>%
  count(offender_racial_construct)

#== location match power ==
homicide_final_reloaded %>%
  summarise(
    n_distinct(
      location_match
    )
  )
```

The victim groups are *5,626* Black and *10,140* Not Black, which add up to 15,766 records, or about 35.7% Black, so Not Black records outnumber Black records almost two to one. For offenders, there are *5,124* Black, *7,658* Not Black, and *2,984* Unknown. And *location_match* has *3,358* different values.

Since offender race has an *"Unknown"* group, the last check compares it against *solved_status* to see whether *"Unknown"* comes mostly from cases that weren't solved. The `count()` counts each pairing of solved status and offender race, and `group_by` with `mutate` turns each count into a percent of its solved-status group, saved as *status_pct*. The `ungroup()` removes the grouping afterward.

```{r offender-unknown-crosstab}
#| warning: true

# Check offender race against solved cases.

#== offender race by solved status ==
homicide_final_reloaded %>%
  count(
    solved_status,
    offender_racial_construct
  ) %>%
  group_by(
    solved_status
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    status_pct = n / sum(n) * 100
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```

For the unsolved cases (*"No"*), *2,619* of the 2,630 records, or *99.6%*, have an *"Unknown"* offender race. For the solved cases (*"Yes"*), only *365* of 13,136, or *2.78%*, do. So an *"Unknown"* offender race almost always comes from a case that wasn't solved.

<br>

## Build and save the modeling data

From the **reloaded DF**, the `mutate()` with `case_when` adds a new column, *jurisdiction_match*. When *agency_population* is NA, the record gets *"Surrounding Area,"* and `TRUE` catches every other record, giving it *"Within Jurisdiction."* That's saved as the **modeling DF** (`homicide_modeling_df`), and `nrow` and `count` show the number of records and the size of each group. I added this column so the records with no agency population are marked as their own group instead of only showing NA.

```{r build-model-data}
#| warning: true

# Derive surrounding/within jurisdiction predictor.

#== build the dataset ==
homicide_modeling_df <- homicide_final_reloaded %>%
  mutate(
    # (Matt, 2020; Hadley, 2024)
    jurisdiction_match = case_when(
      is.na(agency_population) ~ "Surrounding Area",
      TRUE ~ "Within Jurisdiction"
    )
  )

#== display row count ==
nrow(homicide_modeling_df)

#== display new column ==
homicide_modeling_df %>%
  count(jurisdiction_match)
```

The **modeling DF** still has *15,766* records. Of these, *2,897* are *"Surrounding Area"* and *12,869* are *"Within Jurisdiction,"* which add up to the same total.

Then, I'll check how the missing agency population overlaps with the two groups. The first `filter()` with `is.na` keeps the records with no *agency_population*, and the second uses `!is.na`, where the `!` means "not," so it keeps the records that have one. Each `count()` shows which *jurisdiction_match* groups are in them. Lastly, `count` with `group_by` and `mutate` turns the victim race counts into a percent of each jurisdiction group, saved as *group_pct*, and the `ungroup()` removes the grouping.

```{r jurisdiction-na-check}
#| warning: true

# Check missing agency population overlapping with the jurisdiction groups.

#== missing population ==
homicide_modeling_df %>%
  filter(
    is.na(
      agency_population
    )
  ) %>%
  count(jurisdiction_match)

#== non-missing population ==
homicide_modeling_df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(
      agency_population
    )
  ) %>%
  count(jurisdiction_match)

#== display mix groups ==
homicide_modeling_df %>%
  count(
    jurisdiction_match,
    victim_racial_construct
  ) %>%
  group_by(
    jurisdiction_match
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    group_pct = n / sum(n) * 100
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```

The missing-population check shows that all of its *2,897* records are *"Surrounding Area,"* and the non-missing check shows that all of its *12,869* records are *"Within Jurisdiction,"* so *jurisdiction_match* is just a label for whether *agency_population* is missing. In the *"Surrounding Area"* group, *31.2%* of the victims are Black, compared to *36.7%* in the *"Within Jurisdiction"* group; simply put, Black victims make up a somewhat bigger portion of the *"Within Jurisdiction"* records.

To finish, I'll save the **modeling DF** with `arrow::write_parquet()` as its own Parquet file in the processed data folder, separate from the **final DF**'s file. Then, I'll read it back with `arrow::read_parquet()` and get its number of rows and columns with `dim()`.

```{r modeling-data-to-parquet}
#| warning: true

# Save the modeling dataset as a Parquet file.

#== write to data/processed folder ==
# (Olumide, 2025)
arrow::write_parquet(
  homicide_modeling_df,
  here::here(
    "data",
    "processed",
    "homicide_modeling.parquet"
  )
)

#== display row/col counts ==
## (Olumide, 2025)
arrow::read_parquet(
  here::here(
    "data",
    "processed",
    "homicide_modeling.parquet"
  )
) %>%
  dim()
```

In conclusion, the saved file has *15,766* rows and *35* columns, one more than the *34* columns of the **final DF**, since it adds *jurisdiction_match*.

Lastly, this chunk lists the installed versions of the ten packages in `c()`. You can comment it out to prevent it from running every time the script runs, but I'll leave it executable, so that it prints each package's name and version.

```{r cleaning-package-list}
# Produce the package list for C3 that are included in this file.

#== display package versions ==

sapply(
  c(
    "dplyr",
    "tidyr",
    "lubridate",

    "rmarkdown",
    "sessioninfo"
  ),
  function(p) {

      packageVersion(p)
    )
  }
)
```
